newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain, U.S. attacked for changing minds on HK.
newsitem.headline: Britain, U.S. attacked for changing minds on HK.

text.p: Britain, watchdog of Hong Kong's freedom under Chinese rule, was accused on Thursday of inviting contempt by deciding to attend the swearing-in of a controversial new Beijing-appointed legislature.

After caving in to Beijing pressure to allow more troops into Hong Kong before next week's handover, Britain climbed down again on Wednesday and decided to join the United States in sending representatives to the ceremony.
"If they do this, they just invite contempt," declared pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau.
"What kind of message are they trying to send to the rest of the world," she told Radio Hong Kong.

The British move followed the lead of the United States, which felt pragmatism should prevail and it should send its Hong Kong consul-general to the ceremony, being boycotted by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
A Foreign Office spokesman in London stressed on Wednesday: "This in no way implies approval of the provisional legislature to which we are adamantly opposed."

After Hong Kong is handed back to China on the stroke of midnight on June 30, the legislature handpicked by Beijing takes over from an elected body that won widespread support during the five-year era of democratic reforms in Hong Kong.

The Hong Kong Standard echoed the sense of betrayal voiced by Lau with a cartoon showing pro-democracy activist Martin Lee shouting "They're selling us out" as diplomats trooped into the swearing-in ceremony.
The South China Morning Post said in an editorial: "Had this compromise been reached earlier, yesterday's news might invite less scorn.
"But their attempt to have their cake and eat it means London and Washington have forfeited any right to the moral high ground which they like to claim."

The two officials attending the ceremony will be Britain's new Hong Kong consul Francis Cornish and Hugh Davies, head of the Joint Liaison Group monitoring the situation in Hong Kong under a unique "one country, two systems" formula.
Earlier this week Britain bowed to Beijing after protracted negotiations and agreed to let armed Chinese troop reinforcements come into Hong Kong just before the handover.
On Thursday it faced another diplomatic challenge, trying to persuade other European Union states not to send ministers to the legislature's swearing-in ceremony.
Foreign Secretary Robin Cook scheduled talks with fellow EU states in Luxembourg on Thursday in the hope of working out a compromise.
Australia, New Zealand and Japan have already broken ranks and decided to send top-level representatives to the ceremony.

Tung Chee-hwa, the shipping billionaire picked by Beijing to take over as Hong Kong's chief executive, received a boost on Thursday when the colony's top civil servant quashed speculation she would resign.

Highly popular Chief Secretary Anson Chan, who had earlier hinted she might quit if asked to accept polices that went against her principles, said she had no plans to leave before her scheduled retirement in three years' time.
Chan recently topped a Time Magazine opinion poll as the most popular leader in Hong Kong. Tung came second, ahead of democracy activist Lee.

In an ironical twist to the end of empire, Tung decided to set up a new system of honours to reward those who helped smooth the way to the Chinese handover that spells an end to 156 years of colonial rule.

Just four days after Prince Charles hands out the last knighthoods of the colonial era at an investiture ceremony, Tung will be awarding the "Grand Bauhinia Medal" named after the blossom that is Hong Kong's new emblem.
One of the awards goes to Elsie Tu, an 84-year-old Englishwoman who has crusaded for the underdog in colonial Hong Kong for five decades and is the sole white face on China's new legislature.
